content:
You have decided to remodel your kitchen. Now comes the question every homeowner asks next: how long is this actually going to take.

We have managed kitchen remodels long enough to know the answer is not a single number. It is a sequence of phases, and understanding each one tells you exactly what to expect week by week.

Phase One: Design and Planning

Before any demolition begins, your kitchen remodel starts on paper. This phase typically takes two to three weeks and covers layout decisions, material selections, and finalized drawings.

Rushing this phase is one of the most common mistakes homeowners make. A design decision changed mid construction costs far more in time and money than the same decision made during planning, when nothing has been built yet.

Phase Two: Permits and Approval

Any kitchen remodel involving electrical changes, plumbing relocation, or structural work requires permit approval before construction starts. This phase can take anywhere from one to four weeks depending on the scope of your project and local review times.

I always advise clients to build this timeline into their expectations from day one, rather than treating it as an unexpected delay. A remodel that skips this step to save time often ends up costing more once an inspector flags unpermitted work later.

Phase Three: Demolition

Demolition is fast, usually completing within two to five days depending on the size of your kitchen. This is also the phase where hidden issues sometimes surface, such as outdated wiring behind a wall or water damage under old flooring.

What Often Gets Discovered During Demolition

  • Outdated electrical wiring that does not meet current code
  • Water damage or mold behind cabinets or under flooring
  • Structural issues in walls being removed or altered
  • Plumbing that needs rerouting to match the new layout

Finding these issues early is actually good news. It means they get addressed before new finishes go in, not after.

Phase Four: Rough Construction

This phase covers framing, electrical rough in, plumbing rough in, and any structural work, typically taking one to two weeks. Each piece requires inspection before the next step begins, which is why coordination between trades matters so much here.

We have seen firsthand how projects stall for weeks when plumbing, electrical, and framing crews are not coordinated under one schedule. A general contractor managing all three trades keeps this phase moving without gaps between subcontractors waiting on each other.

Phase Five: Installation and Finishes

Cabinets, countertops, flooring, and appliances go in during this phase, usually taking two to four weeks. This is where your kitchen starts to look like the design you approved months earlier.

Material lead times matter a great deal here. Custom cabinetry or specialty countertops can take weeks to arrive, so ordering early during the design phase prevents this from becoming a bottleneck later in the project.

Phase Six: Final Inspection and Punch List

The last phase covers final inspections, fixing any remaining details, and a final walkthrough, typically taking about one week. A thorough punch list process here ensures nothing gets missed before you move back into a finished kitchen.

A Real Kitchen Remodel, Start to Finish

A homeowner in Tampa expected their kitchen remodel to take six weeks total, based on a rough estimate from an earlier conversation. Once demolition began, outdated wiring behind the original cabinets required a full electrical rough in before installation could proceed.

Because our team coordinates electrical, plumbing, and framing under one schedule, the additional wiring work added only one week to the original timeline instead of the months long delay that often happens when trades are managed separately. The kitchen was completed in seven weeks total, with every phase fully inspected and approved.

How We Keep Kitchen Remodels on Schedule

I prioritize a strategy where one team manages design, permitting, and construction together, so no phase is waiting on a separate company to catch up. Our remodeling services team builds every kitchen timeline around this coordinated approach from the very first consultation.

If you are still deciding whether your project needs a licensed general contractor or a smaller trade specialist, our earlier guide on general contractor versus handyman explains exactly where that line sits.

What to Confirm Before Your Remodel Begins

Before signing anything, make sure your timeline expectations match what is actually written into your contract. Our earlier guide on what to check before signing a construction contract covers exactly what timeline language should look like in writing, not just in conversation.

Final Thoughts

A kitchen remodel moves through six clear phases: design, permitting, demolition, rough construction, installation, and final inspection. Most projects take six to twelve weeks total depending on scope, but a coordinated team keeps unexpected discoveries from turning into months of delay.

faqs.q: How long does an average kitchen remodel take?
faqs.a: Most kitchen remodels take six to twelve weeks from design through final inspection, depending on scope and whether structural changes are involved.

faqs.q: What causes kitchen remodel timelines to run long?
faqs.a: Uncoordinated trades, permit delays, and material lead times are the most common causes of a remodel running past its original schedule.

faqs.q: Can I still use my kitchen during a remodel?
faqs.a: Not typically once demolition begins. Most homeowners set up a temporary kitchen space elsewhere in the home during construction.

faqs.q: Should I order cabinets and countertops before construction starts?
faqs.a: Yes. Ordering during the design phase prevents material lead times from delaying the installation phase later.

faqs.q: What happens if hidden issues are found during demolition?
faqs.a: A licensed contractor addresses issues like outdated wiring or water damage as part of the rough construction phase, which may add time but prevents bigger problems later.
